newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Mkt focus turns to PPI Friday.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Mkt focus turns to PPI Friday.

text.p: Jittery bond market investors were hoping tame producer prices on Friday could take some of the sting out of strong retail sales data that sent prices reeling on Thursday.
Industrial production and capacity utilization also were set for release Friday, but little in the way of encouraging news was expected from a vibrant U.S. manufacturing sector.
PPI was set for release by the Labor Department at 830 EST/1330 GMT and industrial production was due from the Federal Reserve at 915 EST/1415 GMT.

Overall PPI was expected to fall by 0.1 percent in February after a 0.3 percent drop in January. The "core" rate, excluding the volatile food and energy components, was seen rising a mere 0.1 percent after an unchanged reading in January, economists polled by Reuters said.
Also slated for release on Friday were January business inventories, which were expected to be up 0.2 percent after a fall of 0.1 percent the prior month.
"After retail sales whatever inflation numbers we get are just a sideshow, barring a humongous deviation from expectations," said Fred Sturm, economist at Fuji Securities.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has said very candidly that the Fed's in a preemptive strike mode and he's going to be shopping around for imbalances and evidence of wage pressure, Sturm said.
Nonetheless, Sturm said he still expected the Fed would not tighten monetary policy at its March 25 meeting, but wait until more evidence was gathered.

"Right now the only smoking gun he has is wage inflation. Imagine the political implications if the Fed comes out beating up on wage earners," Sturm said. "It's easier to wait and move when you have the justification, and it will come."
Greenspan would rather wait and be armed with one or two more strong NAPM surveys, or rising raw materials costs, for example, he said.
Doug Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc., said there may be room for some bounceback with a benign PPI reading on Friday, given the extensive selloff seen on Thursday.

"The selloff was driven by increased confidence the Fed will tighten this month and that provides a setup for a bounce in the market," Schindewolf said. He still expected the Fed to refrain from acting later this month.

"It's become a close call in that they do seem to be emphasizing the need to be preemptive and forward-looking. But saying it and pulling the trigger are two different things and with the absence of signs of growth generating inflation," Schindewolf said.

Bruce Steinberg, macroeconomics manager at Merrill Lynch & Co., said consumers were on a spree that may not be sustainable. Sales may have been spurred on by mild weather leading to a payback in coming months and tax refunds were running about $8.0 billion more than the same period a year ago, Steinberg said.

Late Thursday afternoon three-month bill rates were up five basis points at 5.11 percent. Six-month bill rates were up four basis points at 5.22 percent. Year bill rates were up five basis points at 5.43 percent.

Two-year notes were down 4/32 at 99-14/32, yielding 6.18 percent. Five-year notes were down 13/32 at 98-25/32, yielding 6.54 percent. Ten-year notes were down 23/32 to 96-22/32, yielding 6.71 percent.
The 30-year bond was trading off a full point lower at 95-24/32 to yield 6.96 percent.
